> appropriation; coming to recognise something as one's own. The Stoic account of how moral concern extends.

Glossary

## oikeiōsis οἰκείωσις

appropriation; coming to recognise something as one's own

Ancient Greek · glossed in English

[Glossary](https://www.philosophydef.com/glossary) / oikeiōsis

A term is not a word. It is a working part of somebody's argument, and the English word usually offered for it is a compromise. This page gives the compromise, the argument, and the reading the sources do not support.

Where it is filed: [Humanity](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/humanity) · [Love](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/love) · [Community](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/community) · [Ethics](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/ethics) · [Justice](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/justice) · [Otherness](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/otherness) · [Relation](https://www.philosophydef.com/themes/relation)

### What the term does

The Stoic account of how moral concern extends. A creature begins by being attached to itself and its own constitution, then to its offspring, then to those who share its household and city, and finally — in the fully developed rational being — to all human beings as such, because they share in reason. Hierocles's image is of concentric circles drawn around a centre which one then works to contract. The doctrine is the Stoic answer to why a rational agent should care about strangers, and it is one of the ancestor ideas of later cosmopolitanism and of modern moral-circles arguments.
